title: Uber & DoorDash
summary: Problems whose patterns are commonly reported in Uber and DoorDash coding interviews, from Easy to Hard. Approximate and hand curated, not an official or verified question list.
lesson:
About this list
- Each problem practices a pattern that candidates commonly describe from Uber and DoorDash technical interviews: routing and transit graphs (BFS, Dijkstra, multi-source spread), weighted job and delivery scheduling, spatial/nearest-neighbor heaps, interval merging, and autocomplete/dispatch caches.
- Problems are grouped Easy, Medium, and Hard so you can warm up on intervals and heaps before tackling multi-constraint shortest paths and DP scheduling.
- The selection is approximate. Interview prompts evolve and vary by team, so treat this track as routing, dispatch, and scheduling pattern practice rather than a prediction of what you will be asked.

What to expect
- Candidates often report graph and grid routing problems (minimum transfers, shortest path with obstacles, multi-source spread, weighted shortest paths) alongside delivery/dasher scheduling (weighted interval DP, single-threaded dispatch queues, k-closest points).
- Modeling the right graph state (e.g., node = route vs. stop, or state = `(cell, remainingObstacles)`) is often the key step that turns an exponential search into a clean BFS/Dijkstra.
- Follow-ups frequently tighten latency or scale constraints, pushing O(n^2) DP or naive graph scans to O(n log n) with binary search or priority queues.

How to prepare
- Decide early what constitutes a graph vertex and when to mark visited (at enqueue for unweighted BFS, at pop with best-distance check for Dijkstra).
- For scheduling problems, sort by end time (or start time) and practice pairing DP with binary search to find the last non-overlapping job.
- Trace disconnected graphs, unreachable targets, and single-element schedules explicitly.
